course.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
course.level: research paper; the short targets curious beginners with no probability background beyond fractions
parts: Part II: The discrete channel with noise
Part V: The rate for a continuous source

units.title: Introduction
units.summary: Sets up a general model of communication (source, transmitter, channel, receiver, destination), argues that the information in a choice from a set should be measured by the logarithm of the number of possibilities, and names the base-2 unit the bit.

units.title: The discrete noiseless channel
units.summary: Defines the capacity of a noiseless channel as the growth rate of the log of the number of allowed signal sequences, computed for telegraphy-like symbol durations.

units.title: The discrete source of information
units.summary: Models a message source as a stochastic process that picks symbols with probabilities, possibly depending on preceding symbols.

units.title: The series of approximations to English
units.summary: Generates artificial text from letter and word statistics of increasing order to show that statistical structure makes output look increasingly like English.

units.title: Graphical representation of a Markoff process
units.summary: Draws sources as state graphs whose edges are labelled with emitted letters and their probabilities.
key_ideas: transitions labelled with letters and probabilities

units.title: Ergodic and mixed sources
units.summary: Restricts attention to ergodic sources, whose long sequences all show the same statistics, and treats mixed sources as combinations of ergodic ones.

units.title: Choice, uncertainty and entropy
units.summary: Asks for a measure of the uncertainty in a choice among outcomes with probabilities p_i, lists three natural requirements, and shows that the only measure meeting them is H = -K sum p_i log p_i, the entropy; illustrates its properties (maximal for equal choices, zero for certainty, additive for successive choices).

units.title: The entropy of an information source
units.summary: Extends entropy to a source producing a sequence of symbols, as entropy per symbol, and shows that long typical sequences number about 2^(H N), each with probability about 2^(-H N).

units.title: Representation of the encoding and decoding operations
units.summary: Describes transmitters and receivers as finite-state transducers and shows that such encoding cannot increase entropy.

units.title: The fundamental theorem for a noiseless channel
units.summary: Proves that a source of entropy H can be sent over a channel of capacity C at any rate below C/H symbols per second and no faster, with a constructive coding argument that assigns shorter binary codes to likelier messages.

units.title: Discussion and examples
units.summary: Works examples, including a four-letter source with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 whose entropy is 7/4 bits per symbol and a code (0, 10, 110, 111) that achieves that average exactly; discusses redundancy and matching a source to a channel.

units.title: Representation of a noisy discrete channel
units.summary: Models noise as a probabilistic map from transmitted to received symbols, so received signals are random functions of what was sent.
units.part: Part II: The discrete channel with noise

units.title: Equivocation and channel capacity
units.summary: Defines equivocation H_y(x) as the receiver's remaining uncertainty about the message, the transmission rate as H(x) - H_y(x), and the capacity of a noisy channel as the maximum of this rate.
units.part: Part II: The discrete channel with noise

units.title: The fundamental theorem for a discrete channel with noise
units.summary: Proves that below capacity there are codes with arbitrarily small error frequency, while above it the equivocation cannot be pushed below H - C.
units.part: Part II: The discrete channel with noise

units.title: Discussion
units.summary: Interprets the theorem: redundancy added in the right way lets messages be recovered despite noise, at the cost of delay.
units.part: Part II: The discrete channel with noise

units.title: Example of a discrete channel and its capacity
units.summary: Computes the capacity of a three-symbol channel where the first symbol always arrives intact and the other two are swapped with probability q, by choosing the input probabilities that maximize the rate.
units.part: Part II: The discrete channel with noise

units.title: The channel capacity in certain special cases
units.summary: Derives capacity formulas for channels whose noise treats every input symbol alike (symmetric channels), including the binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p.
units.part: Part II: The discrete channel with noise

units.title: An example of efficient coding
units.summary: Shows a block code on seven binary symbols that corrects any single error, matching a noisy channel exactly.
units.part: Part II: The discrete channel with noise

units.title: Appendix 1: Growth of the number of blocks of symbols
units.summary: Shows the number of allowed symbol blocks grows like the power of the largest root of a determinant equation, justifying the channel capacity formula.

units.title: Appendix 2: Derivation of H = -sum p log p
units.summary: Proves that the three requirements of Section 6 force the logarithmic form of entropy.

units.title: Appendix 3: Theorems on ergodic sources
units.summary: Proves the typical-sequence results of Section 7 for ergodic sources by applying the law of large numbers to the paths taken through the source's state graph.
key_ideas: law of large numbers on paths

units.title: Appendix 4: Maximizing the rate for a system of constraints
units.summary: Finds the transition probabilities that make a constrained source achieve the channel capacity.

units.title: Sets and ensembles of functions
units.summary: Introduces ensembles of continuous functions with probability measures as the continuous analogue of sources.

units.title: Band limited ensembles of functions
units.summary: Uses the sampling theorem to represent a band-limited signal by 2TW numbers.

units.title: Entropy of a continuous distribution
units.summary: Defines differential entropy, notes it depends on the coordinate system, and shows Gaussian distributions maximize it for a given variance.

units.title: Entropy of an ensemble of functions
units.summary: Defines entropy per degree of freedom and per second for continuous ensembles and introduces entropy power.

units.title: Entropy loss in linear filters
units.summary: Computes how a linear filter changes the entropy of an ensemble through the log of its gain.

units.title: Entropy of a sum of two ensembles
units.summary: Bounds the entropy power of the sum of two independent ensembles between the sum of their entropy powers and the sum of their average powers.

units.title: The capacity of a continuous channel
units.summary: Defines the rate and capacity of a channel with continuous signals and noise.

units.title: Channel capacity with an average power limitation
units.summary: Derives C = W log((P + N)/N) for white Gaussian noise with average power limit P.

units.title: The channel capacity with a peak power limitation
units.summary: Bounds capacity when the transmitter has a peak rather than average power limit.

units.title: Fidelity evaluation functions
units.summary: Introduces a fidelity criterion to say how closely a continuous message must be reproduced.
units.part: Part V: The rate for a continuous source

units.title: The rate for a source relative to a fidelity evaluation
units.summary: Defines the rate a continuous source needs for a given fidelity and proves it is achievable over a channel of at least that capacity.
units.part: Part V: The rate for a continuous source

units.title: The calculation of rates
units.summary: Computes the rate needed to reproduce a white-noise source within a mean-square error, showing it equals the bandwidth times the log of the ratio of signal power to allowed error.
units.part: Part V: The rate for a continuous source

units.title: Appendix 5: Entropy under transformations of ensembles
units.summary: Proves how the entropy of an ensemble of functions changes when the ensemble passes through an invertible operation, the result used for linear filters.

units.title: Appendix 6: Entropy power of a sum
units.summary: Proves the upper and lower bounds on the entropy power of a sum of two ensembles stated in Section 23, using white noise as the maximum-entropy case.

units.title: Appendix 7: A general definition of rate and capacity
units.summary: Sketches a measure-theoretic definition of rate and capacity for general signal spaces.
units.part: Part V: The rate for a continuous source
